analysis.one_liner: Lets the Labor Department fine employer health plans that shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 with 11 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never left the House Education and the Workforce Committee and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires employer health plans to cover mental health and substance use care on equal terms with physical care. But no agency can currently fine plans that break that rule, so violations often go unpunished. This bill would let the Department of Labor impose civil monetary penalties on plan sponsors, administrators, and insurers that fail the parity requirement, and it would take effect for plan years starting a year after passage.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families covered by employer health plans who today face tighter limits, higher copays, or narrower networks for mental health and substance use treatment than for physical care. Fining plans that violate parity gives insurers a concrete financial reason to cover this care on equal terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer health plans seeking mental health care

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA's civil monetary penalty provisions so the Department of Labor can penalize plan sponsors, plan administrators, and insurers that fail to meet the mental health and substance use disorder parity requirements.
It carves parity enforcement out of ERISA's general limits on Labor Department enforcement, letting the Secretary directly enforce the mental health parity rule against plans.
The penalty authority would apply to plan years beginning more than one year after enactment, giving plans time to come into compliance before fines could start.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and insurers that currently restrict mental health coverage would face fines and compliance costs if the bill passed, and plans that had to expand coverage would pay for that care. Some of that cost could surface in premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and health insurers violating parity

drawbacks.text: Civil monetary penalties apply to plan sponsors and administrators, not just insurers, so employers could face liability for parity violations, and some compliance costs could flow into premiums for workers.
The bill addresses enforcement of an existing rule but does not change what the parity rule itself requires, so it would not fix coverage gaps that stem from how the rule is written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: a rule with no fine behind it is a rule plans can often ignore, and this puts a real price on shortchanging mental health care. The cost is employer and insurer compliance, some of which may reach workers through premiums. Weighing against the harm of people being denied or priced out of needed mental health treatment, the trade is favorable, though the bill leaves the underlying parity rules untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and no markup, vote, or further action ever followed; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Donald Norcross introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2023 on May 30, 2023, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which held jurisdiction over ERISA.
That referral was the last action on the bill; the full action history shows no committee consideration, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers continue to face no federal fines for violating mental health parity, so plans that restrict this care bear no penalty for it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plans that skimp on mental health coverage

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee for consideration, and it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan support from the start: 10 of its 11 cosponsors were Democrats and 1, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, was a Republican, and it received no committee action at all.

industries.note: Insurers would face Labor Department fines for the first time if they fail to cover mental health and substance use care on equal terms with physical care. Their interest in avoiding enforcement runs against patients who need that care.

Employers as plan sponsors could be fined for parity violations, adding liability and compliance costs. But workers who actually get parity coverage as a result may be healthier and better served, which is why the sponsors wrote the bill.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: Plans forced to cover mental health care on equal terms would expand patients' ability to pay for therapy, medication, and addiction treatment.
